# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Contemporary Narrative Review

## Introduction and epidemiology

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy resulting from the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils in the myocardium. It is most commonly associated with light-chain (AL) amyloidosis and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis, either hereditary or wild-type. Long considered rare, ATTR cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) is now recognized as an important and underdiagnosed cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), particularly in older adults [1,2]. A landmark histological study established that wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis is a cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, helping to reframe the disease as common rather than exceptional [3]. Wider recognition has been driven by the advent of non-invasive diagnosis and the emergence of disease-modifying therapy [4,5].

## Pathophysiology

In ATTR amyloidosis, the liver-derived tetrameric transport protein transthyretin dissociates and misfolds. In the hereditary (variant) ATTR subtype, pathogenic variant subunits destabilize the TTR tetramer, whereas in the wild-type ATTR subtype dissociation, misfolding, and aggregation are caused by age rather than a mutation. Misfolded monomers or oligomers of transthyretin are deposited in the myocardium, leading to cardiomyopathy and symptoms of heart failure, including dyspnea, fatigue, orthostatic hypotension, and syncope. Infiltration of the conduction system can lead to bundle-branch block, atrioventricular block, sinoatrial disease, and atrial fibrillation [6]. In AL amyloidosis, a clonal plasma-cell population produces amyloidogenic immunoglobulin light chains; misfolded immunoglobulin light chains, produced by an abnormal clonal proliferation of plasma cells, deposit in the extracellular matrix of multiple organs [7], with direct light-chain cardiotoxicity contributing to a particularly aggressive course.

## Diagnosis

A high index of suspicion remains essential, as the disease is frequently missed [8]. Once CA is suspected, the cornerstone of evaluation is exclusion of a monoclonal protein. With reasonable clinical suspicion from history, ECG, echocardiogram, or cardiac MRI, clinicians are encouraged first to rule out AL amyloidosis via monoclonal protein screening; if negative, nuclear bone scintigraphy and genetic testing are then completed to categorize patients as ATTRv-CM or ATTRwt-CM [9].

Bone-avid radiotracer scintigraphy is central to non-invasive ATTR diagnosis. The semiquantitative Perugini scale grades myocardial uptake relative to bone [10], and a pivotal multicenter study demonstrated that substantial cardiac radiotracer uptake (Perugini grade >1) on bone scintigraphy yields a specificity of 100% for cardiac ATTR amyloidosis when plasma cell disease is excluded [11]. This established that because of the limited specificity of echocardiography and the traditional requirement for histological confirmation, technetium-labeled bone scintigraphy can localize to myocardial amyloid deposits and be used to diagnose cardiac ATTR amyloidosis non-invasively [11]. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance complements scintigraphy; native T1 mapping and extracellular volume (ECV) quantification enable tissue characterization and prognostication, with every 3% increase in myocardial extracellular volume corresponding to a 16% relative increase in mortality risk [12,13].

## Prognosis and staging

Cardiac biomarkers underpin risk stratification, especially in AL disease. The Mayo 2012 model divides patients based on three biomarkers: high-sensitivity troponin T, NT-proBNP, and the difference between involved and uninvolved serum free light chains (dFLC) [14], yielding stages I–IV with median survival declining markedly across stages [15]. In ATTR disease, scintigraphic and imaging-based staging and the natural history of untreated disease confirm a progressive, fatal trajectory absent therapy [16].

## Treatment

### Transthyretin stabilizers

The pivotal ATTR-ACT trial transformed ATTR-CM management. In patients with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, tafamidis was associated with reductions in all-cause mortality and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations and reduced the decline in functional capacity and quality of life compared with placebo [17]. Acoramidis, a higher-affinity stabilizer, followed. Acoramidis is a high-affinity TTR stabilizer that inhibits dissociation of tetrameric TTR and leads to more than 90% stabilization across the dosing interval as measured ex vivo, and the phase 3 ATTRibute-CM trial demonstrated favorable hierarchical clinical outcomes [18].

### Gene silencing and editing

RNA-interference therapeutics reduce hepatic TTR synthesis. In APOLLO-B, treatment with patisiran over 12 months preserved functional capacity, health status, and quality of life in patients with ATTR cardiac amyloidosis [19]. The subcutaneous siRNA vutrisiran subsequently showed mortality benefit; the HELIOS-B trial showed that vutrisiran was effective at preventing deaths and adverse events among patients with ATTR-CM [20]. Gene editing offers a potentially one-time approach: NTLA-2001 is an in vivo CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing agent designed to treat ATTR amyloidosis by reducing serum TTR, and its administration was associated with only mild adverse events and led to decreases in serum TTR through targeted knockout of TTR [21].

### AL amyloidosis therapy

For AL disease, plasma-cell–directed therapy is paramount. In the ANDROMEDA trial, the addition of subcutaneous daratumumab to bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone resulted in significantly better outcomes in newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis [22], establishing daratumumab-based therapy as standard of care.

## Conclusion

CA has been transformed from a rare, untreatable diagnosis into an increasingly recognized and treatable condition. Non-invasive imaging algorithms permit earlier diagnosis [9,11], while stabilizers, gene silencers, gene editing, and improved AL therapies have reshaped prognosis [17–22]. Lower placebo-group mortality in more recent trials than in earlier treatment groups suggests improvements in amyloid care, including earlier diagnosis [23]. Ongoing priorities include presymptomatic detection [1], refined risk stratification [24,25], management of concomitant aortic stenosis [26], and equitable access to costly disease-modifying agents [27–30].
